taxonomyNote: NatureServe follows the Turtle Taxonomy Working Group (2021) in recognizing two subspecies and treating P. floridensis as a distinct species, while Crother (2017) recognizes P. suwanniensis as a separate species; Animal Diversity Web lists the species as Eastern River Cooter.
fieldMarks: Shell up to about 43.7 cm, flattened, elongated and oval with light and dark brown markings plus green, yellow, brown and black patterns.
Hatchlings 27-39 mm and bright green with light markings; markings darken with age.
Females larger (mean carapace about 287 mm) than males (about 223 mm); males have flatter shells and elongated foreclaws.
behavior: Active about April-October across most of the range; hibernates in mud at the bottom of rivers, lakes and ponds in colder areas.
Mostly herbivorous, eating aquatic vegetation, algae and pondweeds; juveniles take more crayfish and animal prey.
Basks by day and nests on land within about 30 m of water; males court females by stroking their faces with long claws.
habitat: Permanent rivers and lakes with current, aquatic vegetation, basking sites and rocky bottoms; occasionally ponds, springs, swamps and brackish tidal marshes.
range: Eastern and central United States: northern Ohio south to northern Florida, eastern Virginia west to eastern Texas, with disjunct populations in the New River (VA/WV) and Tennessee River. Introduced in Europe (Spain) through the pet trade. Not native to Canada.
